title: The Post-18 Project: Happily HEVA after
summary: Antony Moss outlines a new index that shows some universities are closing gaps between poorer and privileged students – but most of the data is hidden
full_text:
“The Japanese have a saying,” Sean Connery drawls in the 1993 crime thriller Rising Sun, “‘Fix the problem, not the blame.’”

The Japanese do not, in fact, have this saying: it rests on a double meaning of the word “fix” that the Japanese language does not make, so it is almost certainly an English coinage, given artificial weight by its ascription to a different culture.

Perhaps it is scepticism about its provenance that has prevented high-minded professors and evidence-informed policymakers from applying it within English higher education, because apply there it does not. Pretty much all that system is currently concerned with is finding out whose fault something is and appending the blame to a person, institution, or policy, and considering that sufficient to resolve the issue.

Take the matter of funding, high on everyone in the sector’s worry list right now. For the past three years, the HE regulator, the Office for Students (OfS), has publicly enumerated how many institutions on its register are in dire financial trouble. The Department for Education has been very clear that it will not “bail out” any such institution if (more likely, when) they reach the end of the financial road. Financial instability is the fault of the individual provider, it seems clear, and it is for them alone to resolve.

Against this, pressured institutions point the finger back at government: on the one hand, a decade-long unwillingness to raise the value of the government-imposed fee cap, on the other, a recent willingness to actively dissuade international students (who are not covered by that cap) from attending English universities – and let us not even begin to talk about national insurance rises, deliberately underfunded research commissions, or reductions in an already shrunken central grant.

Perhaps it is natural to focus on these things. Fee caps, regulatory conditions, financial strategies – each has an author, and an author can be argued with, lobbied, replaced. Find who made the decision, change the decision (and probably get rid of the person at the same time), and all will be well.

That assumes, of course, a linear causal connection from the decisions made to the outputs generated. But there is plenty of evidence that any system can produce “emergent behaviour” – outputs which can only be the result of the interaction of the system’s parts, not ascribed to any one part alone. That output might be planned for – neither water nor heat alone will make a steam engine move, but the creation of steam is not only not a surprise, it is why the engine is built as it is – but it might also be unexpected.

It is likely such unexpected outputs will also be, initially at least, unexplained, else they would have already been accounted for in the design of the system.

In theory, English post-18 education ought to be very good at providing explanations for its outputs. A significant portion of the system is made up of universities, institutions specifically commissioned to create, curate, and communicate knowledge of how and why the world works as it does. Moreover, the past thirty years have seen an intense focus on constructing accountability structures, including an annual survey of all graduating undergraduates, agreements to work on equality issues in return for increased fees, and reports on which students reach the start of their second year, the end of their final year, and professional employment a year or so after leaving.

But despite this over-abundance of data, too little of it is being turned into genuinely useful information, capable of being deployed to generate credible explanations of what is happening in the system.

To its credit, the government has noticed the gap. Its Post-16 Skills White Paper commits ministers to working with the OfS on a way to “measure and compare progress in higher education”, on the model of Progress 8 in schools. We asked Professor Antony Moss to take that commitment at its word, and to show what such a measure could look like if it were built for higher education as it is, and not borrowed wholesale from a school system that works quite differently.

This paper addresses this challenge directly, taking a well-known data set (the statistics for continuation, completion, and attainment) and interrogating it more thoroughly than has previously been done, to create a valuable source of information about the success, or otherwise, of English institutions registered with the OfS in serving the needs of students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

I would draw out two particularly strong contributions which ought to be in front of every senior figure in the sector.

The first is a function of what data is publicly available – in a characteristically modest way, Tony makes the point almost in passing, but the numbers he examines here make it clear that the institutions for which we currently have no data must, in aggregate, have wider gaps in outcomes for less privileged students than the sector as a whole. Only the regulator can correct that, because it holds the unredacted data – but at present, for three-quarters of registered providers we know nothing of their impact on students from free-school-meal backgrounds, because the data cannot be published.

The second point is to say that Tony’s intention-to-treat approach is one of those ideas that is so powerful once outlined that it seems bizarre it has not been presented before. Because the regulatory metrics are non-cumulative, a provider that loses disadvantaged students in the first year can present a perfectly respectable attainment gap, calculated only across the survivors. The students who left are nobody’s statistic. Tony’s cumulative calculations close that escape hatch: every student a provider chose to recruit stays in the reckoning, and the whole journey becomes attributable to the institution that admitted them.

Thus, the information we can present is powerful – and that which we cannot shows how much more powerful the calculation of these numbers for all providers could be.

However, a word of warning: this paper does not fix the blame. Tony has made no claims here to explain the data he has uncovered. Instead, he has, rightly and usefully, offered a way of better measuring where students from disadvantaged backgrounds are achieving, and where they are not. That is the start of fixing the problem – it may well be that some providers are behaving in reprehensible ways to generate this data, but given that the outcomes show few patterns of institutions by type or region, it seems more plausible that unexamined interactions between different parts of the system are producing emergent behaviour no one wants.

This seems especially likely in the English HE system because of its incoherence – most of its parts are badly or barely governed, and the interplay between them is no one’s responsibility at all. Other work by The Post-18 Project will address this phenomenon and propose solutions. But for now, please read Tony’s excellent and thought-provoking work in the spirit of fixing the problem through greater understanding.

full_text:
Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.

The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.

Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.

Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.

The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.

Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.

“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”

Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.

Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.

She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”

In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.

Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”

In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.

In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.

Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.

In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.

Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”

A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

title: The Guardian view on vocational GCSEs: why now? | Editorial
summary:
Ministers’ commitment to cutting youth unemployment is admirable, but how new qualifications will help is unclear

The first question that should be asked about plans to launch a batch of vocational GCSEs is: how will these differ from the roughly 50 similar courses that already exist? Is this primarily a rebadging exercise, aimed at boosting the qualifications’ status and name recognition, while signalling how seriously non-academic education is taken by Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell? Or is there something the matter with the existing courses that they want to put right?

The first question that should be asked about plans to launch a batch of vocational GCSEs is: how will these differ from the roughly 50 similar courses that already exist? Is this primarily a rebadging exercise, aimed at boosting the qualifications’ status and name recognition, while signalling how seriously non-academic education is taken by Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell? Or is there something the matter with the existing courses that they want to put right?

The independent curriculum review completed last year recommended a moratorium on new technical awards, except where there is an “exceptionally compelling” case for change. It also proposed that the Department for Education analyse existing ones, including how well they prepare pupils for 16-19 education; no such research has appeared.

Last year, around 170,000 16-year-olds in England and Wales took a level 2 BTec qualification alongside GCSEs – the two most popular being health and sport and leisure. They are also studied by post-16 students at further education colleges. While the number of entries is dwarfed by the overall annual total of 5.7m GCSEs, it is not the case that all individual GCSEs have higher take-up. In 2024, for example, just 6,723 pupils took a GCSE in dance.

The fact that technical awards are not on the radar of many pupils and parents does not mean that they lack value. The low awareness of vocational options is widely recognised as a problem and was cited by Pepe Di’Iasio, the general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, in response to this week’s announcement. Clearer signposting is expected to be among the recommendations of a review chaired by Charles Clarke, a former education secretary, when it is published later this autumn.

The second question about vocational GCSEs is how they will relate to the plans for new V-levels (level 3 qualifications like A-levels), to which the government is already committed. V-levels are due to replace all existing vocational level 3s apart from T-levels, after ministers rejected a campaign aimed at saving some older courses. Will vocational GCSEs be viewed as stepping stones to the new V-level courses? If not, how will duplication and repetition be avoided?

For schools, the key issues will be practical. Construction is one of the new GCSEs promised. But there are already many vacancies for construction‑related college teaching positions and it is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from – or whether training teachers for new subjects should take priority over existing shortages.

The government’s commitment to getting more young people into jobs is admirable, and ministers are right to push for more work‑experience opportunities. But given the difficulties in this area encountered by T-level students – which led to a watering down of the initial requirement for a placement – it is doubtful whether the aim of getting large numbers of 14- to 16-year-olds into workplaces is realistic.

title: When Nontraditional Students Become the Norm
summary:
When Nontraditional Students Become the Norm Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/24/2026 - 03:00 AM Bryan Ashton of Trellis Strategies discusses what colleges need to rethink as “nontraditional” students increasingly reflect today’s college population. Byline(s) Joshua Bay When Nontraditional Students Become the Norm
Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

Bryan Ashton of Trellis Strategies discusses what colleges need to rethink as “nontraditional” students increasingly reflect today’s college population.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Adult learners, working students, student parents, transfer students and first-generation students are often grouped under the broad umbrella of “nontraditional” students. While their experiences differ, they also highlight the various ways higher education is, or isn’t, designed around the realities of students’ lives.

Many of these students are navigating similar pressures: balancing college with work and family responsibilities, managing financial challenges and figuring out systems that weren’t necessarily built with them in mind. And as these experiences become increasingly common across higher education, they raise a bigger question: If so-called nontraditional students reflect the reality of today’s college population, does it still make sense to call them nontraditional?

Bryan Ashton, chief strategy and growth officer at Trellis and head of Trellis Strategies, a nonprofit organization that works with colleges and universities across the country, joined Inside Higher Ed student success reporter Joshua Bay on Voices of Student Success for the final episode of our series on nontraditional students.

Follow us on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

Here are five key takeaways from Ashton on what today’s students need and how colleges can better design around their lives.

“Nontraditional” students have become the norm.

Ashton noted that as more people pursue postsecondary education later in life, the characteristics once associated with “nontraditional” students have become increasingly common across the broader student population.

“Even the traditional students are having characteristics of what we would traditionally call nontraditional,” Ashton said, noting that Trellis Strategies uses the term “modern learners” to encompass both traditional-age students and adult learners balancing education with work, family responsibilities and other demands.

“That kind of perspective on how we serve learners is probably more fitting for where students are today than trying to think about this arbitrary cutoff of a 25-year-old or somebody who’s transferred in, but rather that our systems need to evolve to meet the needs of all learners, and that those needs look different than they did 10 to 15 years ago for many of our students,” Ashton said.

College is only one part of students’ lives.

Drawing on the Trellis Strategies 2025 Student Financial Wellness Survey, Ashton highlighted that one in five students identify as a parent or caregiver and 34 percent consider themselves workers who go to school rather than students who work.

“When we start to think about these different personas that students have, that really informs how they engage with postsecondary education and training,” Ashton said, adding that students are increasingly engaging with their education in a “nonlinear” fashion, meaning attending consecutive semesters may not always align with how they navigate college.

“When you start to think about the trade-offs of ‘Do I go to class or do I take care of a child who’s sick and can’t go into a childcare setting?’ Those other primary personas always will weed out the academic experience,” he said.

Ashton also noted that employment can create a push-and-pull for students who need to work to afford college and their broader living expenses, even when their jobs make it more difficult to fit classes into their schedules.

“We know that [students] need to work to be able to close those gaps, but oftentimes employment and class schedules can come into conflict,” Ashton said.

“Something that we lose a lot in conversation is this isn’t just students that are engaging with one employer; they’re engaging with sometimes two employers or multiple gig employers,” he added. “As they try to navigate these employment schedules with academic schedules, it becomes a semester-by-semester puzzle that they have to put together to be able to attend class.”

Financial instability can become an academic problem.

Ashton said higher education leaders thinking about student engagement and persistence also need to consider how financial stability affects whether students are able to remain enrolled and ultimately complete their education.

“It’s impossible to separate those two conversations,” Ashton said. “When I ask learners why they left an institution, finances, both direct and indirect costs, are always some of the leading causes of why students say that they don’t persist.”

He noted that the Pell Grant, a need-based federal subsidy for undergraduate students, covers only a fraction of the total cost of attendance, but the growing financial pressure students face isn’t driven solely by tuition and other direct college costs.

“What has increased exponentially is the cost of living,” Ashton said. “And it’s unfortunate because this isn’t something that institutions have a ton of control over, but it’s a super real reality for the students that they’re enrolling.”

Ashton also pointed to Trellis survey data showing that about 52 percent of students worry about having enough money to cover their monthly expenses, and 21 percent said they ran out of money eight or more times in a single year. Those recurring financial gaps, he said, have contributed to students turning to products such as credit cards and buy-now-pay-later services to cover expenses.

“We see both the macro, which is that unmet need is really driving unsustainable financial gaps that students can’t cover to stay enrolled and the micro, which is that there’s month-to-month stress and anxiety that’s coming with not being able to meet basic needs,” Ashton said. “That creates this perfect storm for student financial stress and then has a persistent impact after that.”

Rethinking institutional design can reduce student barriers.

Ashton noted that higher education has historically expected students to center their lives around their education, pointing to the rigidity of structures such as the academic calendar that institutions can struggle to adapt around students’ changing needs.

“We’re really in a position where, as these other personas—a worker who goes to school, a student parent—become more and more the primary persona, we have an obligation to figure out how we can fit education into people’s lives,” Ashton said.

While some challenges, such as rising housing costs, lie largely outside an institution’s control, colleges have more control over other barriers, Ashton said. Offering online or hybrid courses, for example, could reduce the transportation burden for students as gas prices rise.

“There’s a redesign component around what do institutions control that is super important,” Ashton said. “We’ve asked students to navigate a really complex system, and we haven’t necessarily thought about, ‘How do we make that user experience easier?’”

One of the most underappreciated interventions available to colleges, Ashton said, is the course schedule.

“We sort of refer to it as the highway through which everything else is scaffolded on,” Ashton said. “I really can’t do a great job of helping students to manage employment with academics if they don’t have predictability when their scheduled courses are going to be.”

“Those are where we’re really thinking about ‘How do we take those points and make that kind of more holistic systemwide change, while still allowing for certain student populations to get those targeted interventions that help to create and serve some of the unique circumstances that they’re facing?’” he added.

Colleges need to design for the students they actually serve.

Ashton said part of the challenge of redesigning higher education around today’s students is determining what comes first: changing how institutions define student success or altering the structures attached to that definition.

“A lot of what we’ve built the environment around is how we define student success … [but] the future of education and training is much more nonlinear, with people starting and stopping,” Ashton said. “It’s a lot more about credit mobility, learning mobility and how we take experiences from one institution to another.”

For Ashton, the biggest takeaway is the need for institutions to flip their perspective: Instead of asking students to fit their lives into an institution’s model, colleges should ask how they can make that model fit into students’ lives.

“If we can begin to ask that question as we’re looking at institutional policies or as we’re looking at the experience that students are having on campus, that can become a really good test to say, ‘Are we evolving to meet the needs of modern learners?’” Ashton said.

title: N.S. teacher charged with sexually assaulting student at school
summary: Matthew Donahoe, 53, faces charges in incidents alleged to have occurred this school year. RCMP have identified other victims and say there may be more.
full_text:
A Nova Scotia teacher is facing a slew of charges, including sexual assault involving a student at the school where he taught, and RCMP say they have identified other victims in similar alleged incidents.

Matthew Donahoe, 53, of Bible Hill, N.S., has been charged with sexual assault, sexual interference, assault with a weapon, two counts of assault by choking, four counts of assault, and administering a noxious substance.

RCMP said the charges relate to multiple victims, but would not say how many.

Police also would not share information about the age or gender of the victims, what grade Donahoe taught or whether the affected students were in his class.

Donahoe is a teacher at Dr. W.A. MacLeod Consolidated School in Riverton, N.S. The school serves students in pre-primary to Grade 8.

RCMP said they received an initial report of an assault on Sept. 10, just five days into the school year. During their investigation, they identified other victims of similar alleged assaults.

All the alleged assaults occurred within the 2026-27 school year and took place inside the school, during the school day, RCMP said.

According to police, the Chignecto Central Regional Centre for Education removed Donahoe's access to the school and students at the time of the initial allegation of an assault.

In a statement, the regional education centre said the charges are "deeply troubling" and it takes the matter "very seriously."

The centre had supports available at the school on Thursday and will continue to do so into next week. The school has notified families that Donahoe has been placed on leave, the statement said.

RCMP said there may be more victims, and said investigators will use a supportive and trauma-informed approach to investigating.

"Investigators understand that coming forward may be difficult," Cpl. Carlie McCann told CBC News.

"We want you to understand that we can go at the pace and use the process that is going to work for you or your loved ones or the people you care for and we understand that this maybe a difficult thing for people to bring forward."

McCann said victims can come forward to police without deciding immediately if they want to be involved in the full investigation or court process. She said resources are available to help.

Donahoe was arrested Wednesday.

He appeared in Pictou provincial court on Thursday afternoon with a white beard and collared shirt. Families of students also attended court.

Some of Donahoe's release order conditions include:

No contact with persons under age 18.

He's not allowed to attend places youths frequent.

He has to abide by a curfew.

He must reside with a surety in Dartmouth, N.S.

Attending court when directed.

Remaining in Nova Scotia.

Not being within 500 metres of any home, school or workplace of 10 named individuals.

Not possessing any weapons.

Not attending any public park, school ground, daycare centre, swimming pool, playground, skating rink, community centre, recreation centre or anywhere persons under the age of 18 are present or might reasonable be expected to be present.

Donahue is due back at court on Oct. 19.

title: ‘Jaldi kar, Panvel nikalna hai’: Student’s joke leads to ugly spat with Nirma professor
summary: During a comedy event at Nirma University, a student's remark led to a confrontation with a professor. The professor allegedly grabbed the student's collar and issued a threat in response. The National Students' Union of India demanded an apology from the professor and called for an impartial inquiry into the incident. The university has not yet publicly responded to these demands or commented on the incident.
full_text:
Image Credit: X ( A professor called a student sitting in the audience on stage and grabbed him by the collar)

AHMEDABAD: A student's alleged remark, "Jaldi kar, Panvel nikalna hai," during a comedy show at Nirma University in Ahmedabad has led to a controversy after a video purportedly showing a professor grabbing the student's collar went viral on social media. The incident allegedly took place during 'Technofora 2026', a three-day event organised by students of the university's Institute of Technology from September 18 to 20.

What happened during the event

According to the claims surrounding the video, a professor and head of the electrical and instrumentation department was addressing students when the student shouted the remark, referring to a dialogue from the Bollywood film 'Golmaal'. The professor then called the student on stage and allegedly grabbed him by the collar, as seen in the video. The professor is also heard threatening the student in the video, saying, "I can go to any extent. The day you dare to insult any faculty member of the Nirma University campus, you are gone forever." The video purportedly shows the incident during a stand-up comedy show featuring comedian Rajat Sood.

NSUI demands apology, inquiry

The Congress-affiliated National Students' Union of India (NSUI) has demanded an apology from the professor and an inquiry into the incident. NSUI state vice president Vedant Tomar said, “The professor must apologise to the student and the university should conduct an impartial inquiry into the incident.” Bhavik Solanki, national coordinator of the NSUI, claimed in a statement that the student was subjected to inappropriate behaviour and also demanded an apology from the professor and an inquiry. The NSUI said it would hold a protest if its demands were not met.

University yet to respond

The private university did not respond to an email seeking its comment on the incident. The circumstances leading to the confrontation, including the student's alleged remark and the professor's response, could not be independently verified.

title: When the Tool Trips You Up: LiveBinder Glitches, Fixes, and Student Problem Solving
summary:
On paper, LiveBinder seemed ideal for my undergraduate literacy methods course: free, accessible, and built for collaborative content creation. Students could upload documents, annotate websites, and learn from peers, all course goals. I expected the tool to integrate seamlessly. Mostly it did, until it didn’t. Adopting the popular adage of failing forward and falling back […]

The post When the Tool Trips You Up: LiveBinder Glitches, Fixes, and Student Problem Solving appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
On paper, LiveBinder seemed ideal for my undergraduate literacy methods course: free, accessible, and built for collaborative content creation. Students could upload documents, annotate websites, and learn from peers, all course goals. I expected the tool to integrate seamlessly. Mostly it did, until it didn’t. Adopting the popular adage of failing forward and falling back on my mother’s wisdom of making lemonade out of lemons, below I describe three problems that emerged, the solutions used, and practical tips other educators can apply immediately.

Problem 1: What Email Address Did You Use?

What happened: Adding students as collaborators required an email address they used to register. In class, I asked students to create accounts and come to the teaching station to enter their addresses. Several students couldn’t remember which email they’d used. After trying multiple addresses with no luck, a lot of students were stuck, which only raised frustration and ate up class time.

What I changed: I now require students to register before class and submit the email they used on a simple Google Form (or add it to a secured master list I maintain). I also include email registration as an item on my course checklist, so students know it’s required.

Tip: Make registration and email collection a pre-class task. Store addresses in a password-protected document and briefly explain how you’ll safeguard the list (adhering to FERPA and privacy practices as appropriate).

Problem 2: Have I Read This Before? (Work Visible = Unintended Copying)

What happened: LiveBinder’s collaborative pages allowed groups to see earlier submissions. Using a read-aloud and a Three-Level Guide assignment (Herber, 1978), groups were to analyze a children’s book at literal, interpretive, and applied levels. After the first two groups posted thoughtful guides, later groups began to rephrase those postings rather than produce original analyses, a clear case of easy access squelching creativity that Khan and Alamri (2017) warn can happen when collaborative tools are not scaffolded appropriately.

What I changed: To preserve independent work, I blocked the binder page (or otherwise restricted access) until all groups had completed their drafts. Once every group submitted evidence of completion, I opened the page so they could post simultaneously. Where platform controls are limited, an instructor-only submission route (e.g., a private folder or LMS dropbox) can serve the same purpose.

Tip: If student work will be visible during the activity, build in procedures to keep drafts private until all groups have finished or require process artifacts (e.g., notes, screenshots of planning) that document independent thinking.

Problem 3: Yikes — Disappearing Posts (Concurrent Edits)

What happened: Opening the page for everyone to post at once removed the copying problem but introduced overwrites. Groups on the same Wi‑Fi and the same LiveBinder page kept cancelling each other’s posts. Asking students to wait until the previous group saved helped at first, but by the third posting some earlier work had vanished again.

What I changed: Students discovered a simple workflow: after a group posted, the next group refreshed the LiveBinder page before adding their work. To reduce risk further, I started assigning each group a distinct page or folder when possible or requiring uniquely named files so simultaneous posting wouldn’t affect others. These small changes eliminated the disappearing-post problem.

Tip: When using a tool without robust concurrent-edit safeguards, avoid having multiple groups edit the exact same page at the same time. Use separate pages/folders, enforce unique file naming, or stagger submissions with a refresh rule.

Would I Use LiveBinder Again?

Yes. Learning to problem-solve is necessary for the real-world. Problems often aren’t obvious, nor do they always have easy solutions. Yet, as human beings, we must be able to think through issues and work out how best to approach them. This teaching experience became that kind of learning moment. Students weren’t just using technology; they were identifying setbacks and designing workable solutions. Despite the frustrations, the tool supported collaborative content-building and, more importantly, created opportunities for students to practice critical thinking and problem-solving. The technical hiccups only highlighted the need for small, deliberate process changes; those scaffolds made the technology serve learning rather than hinder it. As Khan and Alamri (2017) argue, technology can help students become critics and creators rather than mere consumers (provided teachers anticipate workflow and privacy issues). And the Three-Level Guide task (Herber, 1978) provided an effective structure for prompting literal, interpretive, and applied analysis.

Classroom-Ready Checklist

Require account creation and collect the registration email before class (Google Form or secured master list).

Keep student drafts private until all groups finish (block pages, use instructor-only folders, or set a simultaneous publish time).

Prevent overwrites by assigning separate pages/folders per group (one folder per group), enforcing unique file names (use a naming convention), or setting a refresh/staggered-posting rule (stagger posts by X minutes).

Have a backup submission method (LMS dropbox, Google Drive, or screenshots) in case the primary tool fails.

Final Takeaway

Digital tools like LiveBinder can expand collaborative learning, but they usually need a bit of logistical scaffolding, i.e., clear registration procedures, privacy controls for drafts, and simple posting rules to prevent technical collisions. Those upfront steps reduce frustration and create richer opportunities for student thinking. In the end, that is the real payoff.

A recipient of multiple research grants, her scholarship examines looping in higher education, teacher quality, reflective and reflexive inquiry, and sustaining rural community voices, especially those in Appalachia. She is a Faculty Fellow with the Renaissance Foundry Gadugi Fellows Program and served as an expert panelist for the 2026 Horizon Report: Teaching and Learning. An experienced presenter and consultant, her professional activities include workshops, keynotes, webinars, publications, and service at local to international levels. She is editor-in-chief of the International Journal of Childhood Education.

The post Small Moves, Big Impact: Building a Positive Climate in Online Classes appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
When I think of a positive classroom climate, I picture a brightly lit classroom with students sitting around tables, a soft buzz of student discussion, and the teacher facilitating their learning. But I am old-fashioned. Those days are long gone for many of us who teach online or hybrid courses with asynchronous or synchronous components.

One of the challenges that online instructors face is creating a sense of connectedness in which students feel present, “seen,” heard, and part of the learning community. We know student engagement and learning are enhanced when students feel connected—students to the content, students to the instructor, and students to each other. In online environments, social presence is when students perceive that others are real, accessible, and engaged. Researchers such as Garrison (2017) and Lowenthal and Dunlap (2018) have linked increased social presence to higher student satisfaction, stronger participation, and more meaningful learning experiences in online settings. Given this, I offer several strategies to increase social presence and improve your online classroom climate.

First Impressions

The beginning of any course is an essential time for establishing a positive classroom climate. Professors can introduce themselves with a short bio, rather than a professional vita. A photo collage or short video introduction (think Reels on Instagram) can highlight personal and professional experiences and interests that connect you to the content, university, or your students’ experiences.

There are several strategies for students to get to know each other, including posting a text-based introduction, a picture that has meaning for them, or a video introduction. Instructors can use tools within their institution’s learning management system or external tools, such as collaborative documents, to personalize introductions. I teach aspiring school leaders, and some of my favorite introductory prompts are to have students write about their favorite principal or their favorite supervisor. This type of self-disclosure prompt announces to the instructor and their classmates what they value in addition to their background and experiences. It creates a climate that allows students to show their authentic selves and take risks as they begin the course.

Creating Community

Almost 30 years ago, Garrison et al. (1999) wrote that, in online environments, social presence can distinguish a collaborative community of inquiry from a simple process of downloading information. The same is true today, and instructors can use numerous strategies to promote a community of inquiry. One of the most powerful exercises to help people feel connected is to get everyone’s voice in the room. This can happen through a check-in question for synchronous sessions or a discussion prompt for asynchronous courses. These prompts can be personal, such as talking about your favorite animal or superpower, or more related to the course content. Instructors can also use reaction emoticons and thumbs up to help students feel appreciated and valued.

A positive classroom climate is built and sustained when students feel comfortable expressing themselves and offering their unique perspectives. Discussion boards can be a great way to build knowledge by having students post and then respond to their classmates, but sometimes they can hurt authentic connections. A response such as “great idea” can squash connections, as it comes across as transactional and compliance driven. Rather, instructors can encourage and notice more organic and personalized responses.

In Small Teaching Online, Darby and Flowers (2019) remind us, “It’s easy to forget that a name on the screen represents a human being who can benefit from your presence and benefit your learning with their presence” (p. 81). To combat this, instructors can design discussion prompts that encourage debate, allow students to share their perspectives, or discuss a real-life case or scenario without a single, correct answer.

Creating community can be challenging with large groups. Whether through online discussions or breakout rooms in synchronous sessions, smaller groups can enhance students’ social presence and, thus, the classroom climate and learning. I have found that discussion groups of three or four students allow students to be exposed to the ideas of various classmates and enhance student-to-student learning.

In many of my classes, students attend synchronous sessions every other week. After the first session in which everyone introduces themselves, I use breakout rooms once or twice per session. Usually, I let the computer assign the groups so that everyone has a chance to interact with different learners in the class. Then, during the sessions, I give a few extra minutes in the breakout groups so students can reintroduce themselves, have an opportunity to share, and check in with each other about burning issues. Allowing a few extra minutes in breakout rooms lets students share their authentic selves with each other and offer support.

Sustaining Community

In a face-to-face classroom, instructors sustain a positive environment by showing up to class ready and energized. Within a virtual environment, instructors need to check in often and interact in small ways since “too much prolonged silence on our part is a sure way to kill the energy in an online class” (Darby & Flowers, 2019, p. 89). I’ll add that silence can also squash a positive learning environment.

Instructors can use students’ names in their responses, participate in discussions with comments or simple emoticons, and provide timely feedback to let their students know they are present, too. Announcements and short videos are also great ways to connect with students. One of my colleagues introduces each module in her asynchronous classes with a short three-to-five-minute video overview, which her students report helps them feel connected to the class and provides them motivation and inspiration for the week’s learning.

Enhancing a positive learning environment within an online environment only takes small moves: focusing on introductions, allowing for opportunities for real sharing, being present in discussions, and personalizing feedback. It’s never too late to leverage strategies to build connections, community, and a positive climate in your online classes.

Amie Cieminski, EdD, is an associate professor and department chair at the University of Northern Colorado in Greeley, Colorado. Previously, she worked as a teacher, principal, director of professional learning, and school district administrator in several K-12 school districts. Amie teaches educational leadership preparation courses such as the principalship and instructional leadership as well as district level leadership, organizational change, and doctoral research classes for aspiring educational leaders. Her research interests include instructional practices; leadership development; and inclusive, equitable, and socially just leadership.

References

Darby, Flower, and James M. Lang. Small Teaching Online: Applying Learning Science in Online Classes. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 2019.

Garrison, D. Randy. E-Learning in the 21st Century: A Community of Inquiry Framework for Research and Practice. 3rd ed. New York: Routledge, 2017.

Garrison, D. Randy, Terry Anderson, and Walter Archer. “Critical Inquiry in a Text-Based Environment: Computer Conferencing in Higher Education.” The Internet and Higher Education 2, nos. 2–3 (1999): 87–105.

title: Digitalisierung in der Kardiologie: Zwischen Fortschritt und Frust
summary: KI revolutioniert die Kardiologie, doch die Digitalisierung hinkt. Visionen treffen auf frustrierende Realität im deutschen Gesundheitswesen.

Inhaltsverzeichnis

.

Wie weit Möglichkeiten und Alltag in der digitalen Kardiologie auseinanderliegen, zeigen die Herztage der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Kardiologie (DGK). Unter dem Titel „Künstliche Intelligenz im Alltag der Kardiologie“ trafen die Vision eines Krankenhauses ohne Tastatur und der Frust über PDF-Sammlungen und leere Ordner in der elektronischen Patientenakte aufeinander. Ausgerichtet wurde die Veranstaltung der DGK gemeinsam mit dem Digital Cardiology and Artificial Intelligence Committee der Europäischen Gesellschaft für Kardiologie (ESC).

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Dr. Max Tschochohei, Softwareentwickler bei Google, zeigte zum Einstieg, wie stark die Forschung zu KI-gestützten klinischen Entscheidungsunterstützungssystemen gewachsen ist. In der Klinik greife man dagegen bei schwierigen Fragen zum Smartphone und frage ChatGPT. Oft bekämen sie wohl die richtige Antwort, offiziell dürften sie das aber nicht. Er stellte die Frage, warum solche Systeme noch nicht in der Fläche ankommen.

„Digitalisierung ist noch keine Vernetzung“

Simon Glück, Geschäftsführer der BNK Service GmbH, einer Tochter des Bundesverbands Niedergelassener Kardiologen (BNK), beschrieb die Ausgangslage nüchtern. Die Telematikinfrastruktur (TI) sei Infrastruktur und keine Versorgung. Eine Datenübergabe bringe erst etwas, wenn sich jemand für den nächsten Schritt zuständig fühle.

Sein Beispiel: Eine Klinik entlässt einen Patienten nach einem akuten Koronarsyndrom. Sie weiß, dass er schnell einen Termin beim niedergelassenen Kardiologen benötigt und dass die Lipidsenkung im Blick bleiben muss. Ob diese Information in der Praxis ankommt, stelle aber niemand sicher: „Es gibt kein System dafür“. Außerdem fehlten ein Rückkanal mit Eingangsbestätigung, eine Eskalation bei Warnzeichen („Red Flags“) und eine einheitliche Identifizierung der Patienten. Die Daten seien nicht strukturiert und oft keinem Behandlungsfall zeitlich zugeordnet.

Aus einer stationären Einrichtung habe er gehört, dass dort täglich mehrere Faxe mit Patientendaten eingehen. Man lege sie auf einen Stapel und warte ab, ob der Patient kommt. Eine ähnliche Folie habe er schon vor fast zehn Jahren gezeigt, und seitdem habe sich wenig geändert.

ePA als PDF-Sammlung, kaum Nutzer beim TI-Messenger

Die elektronische Patientenakte (ePA) sei der Anfang eines „Backbones“ für ein medizinisches Informationssystem. Im Moment sei sie aber vor allem eine Sammlung von PDF-Dokumenten, was regelmäßig bemängelt wird. Den größten Nutzen sieht Glück bisher im Medikationsplan. Dann fragte er in den Saal, wer schon einen TI-Messenger nutzt – nur eine Person meldete sich.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Eine Person aus dem Publikum brachte den Messenger Siilo ins Spiel. Doctolib hatte den Dienst übernommen und später in Doctolib Connect umbenannt. Die Übernahme sehe er kritisch. Vergangene Woche habe sie den TI-Messenger genutzt und einen Kollegen angeschrieben, bisher allerdings keine Antwort erhalten.

Glück sprach auch über Daten aus Wearables, digitalen Gesundheitsanwendungen (DiGA) und dem inzwischen vergüteten Telemonitoring bei Herzinsuffizienz. Für diese Daten fehle eine „Brückenfunktion“ in die Versorgung. Er forderte ein „digitales Betriebssystem für den Versorgungspfad“, dazu gehören für ihn eine eindeutige Patientenidentität und Interoperabilität, ein strukturierter Mindestdatensatz, der sich jedoch in der Entwicklung befindet, Register und Feedbackschleifen sowie Regeln für Governance und Kompetenz. Das größte Problem sei bei all den Plänen die Finanzierung. Mit der aktuellen Gesetzgebung „laufen wir eher wieder rückgängig“.

Die Vision der Charité: das Krankenhaus ohne Tastatur

Prof. Gerhard Hindricks vom Deutschen Herzzentrum der Charité (DHZC) trat deutlich offensiver auf. „Die Zukunft der Medizin wird auf digitalen Plattformen entschieden“. Für die nächsten zwei bis drei Jahre erwartet er eine deutliche Beschleunigung. Als Gründe nannte er weniger Regulierung, eine „risikoaffinere Haltung“ und Geld, denn digital aufgestellte Häuser arbeiteten wirtschaftlicher und besser. Die Technik sei nicht das Problem: „Wir haben ein Implementierungsproblem“, so Hindricks.

Künftig soll die Charité zum kontaktlosen und keyboardlosen Krankenhaus werden. Zwanzig Jahre lang habe man Ärzte vor Computer gesetzt, jetzt müsse man sie dort wieder wegholen. Im Neubau des DHZC sollen Patienten, Pflegekräfte und Ärzte freihändig sprechen und dokumentieren. Eine sprachgesteuerte „Ambient AI“ überträgt die Inhalte automatisch in die Systeme. Radarsensoren sollen Biosignale ohne Berührung erfassen. Vernetzt wird über 5G und später 6G, Hindricks verwies dazu auf die Hightech-Agenda der Bundesregierung. KI-Agenten sollen die Abläufe steuern.

Hindricks selbst arbeite schon so: „Ich erstelle keinen Arztbrief mehr, der nicht KI unterstützt ist“. Patientengespräche würden nach ausdrücklicher Zustimmung aufgezeichnet. Auf Knopfdruck gebe es zusätzlich eine Fassung in einfacher Sprache, die der Patient auch versteht. Hindricks sagte außerdem einen Durchbruch der Robotik voraus. Elon Musk möge er nicht, aber was Tesla mit autonomen, adaptiven Robotern mache, „das ist einfach unfassbar“.

„Kritik an Epic von Menschen, die nichts davon verstehen“

Zum Stand der Charité zeigte Hindricks, dass sie auf der HIMSS-Skala für den Digitalisierungsgrad (0 bis 7, hoch ist besser) derzeit auf allen Ebenen bei 0 bis 1 liege. Mit dem Krankenhausinformationssystem (KIS) Epic wolle man auf 5 bis 6 kommen und in fünf Jahren überall 6 bis 7 erreichen. Epic koste zunächst 250 Millionen Euro, „und da sind die Sekundärkosten noch nicht“ eingepreist. Im zweiten Quartal 2029 sollen rund 24.000 Beschäftigte und 3600 Betten auf einen Schlag umgestellt werden. Das sei ein „riesiges Investment“. Wenn es irgendwo ein sinnvolles Invest geben müsse, dann in der Digitalisierung des Gesundheitswesens. Für die Entscheidung sei die Charité kritisiert worden, „von Menschen, die nichts davon verstehen“. Dabei habe ein zuvor defizitäres Haus mit Epic innerhalb von zwei Jahren einen zweistelligen Millionengewinn erreicht, das Klinikum Luzern habe Ähnliches geschafft.

Das Gesundheitswesen braucht laut Hindricks selbstlernende Systeme, die mit jedem Datensatz besser werden. Die Menschen müssten verstehen, „dass da auch der individuelle Datenschutz, wo er depersonalisiert ist, komplett enden muss“. Auch die Grenzen zwischen ambulantem und stationärem Sektor müssten fallen. Krankenhäuser und Niedergelassene hielten sie teils aufrecht, um „Claims abzustecken und Kohle abzusichern, da müssen wir uns ehrlich machen“.

„KI ist besser als die kardiologische Zunft“

Laut Prof. Holger Thiele vom Herzzentrum Leipzig spricht man nicht über die Zukunft, wenn es um KI in der Rhythmusdiagnostik geht. Die KI sei besser als die kardiologische Zunft und werde das Langzeit-EKG für die Suche nach Vorhofflimmern überflüssig machen. Als Belege nannte er Studien, unter anderem aus Nature Medicine. Bei AV-Blöcken, einer gestörten Erregungsleitung zwischen Vorhof und Kammer, und anderen Befunden, gelte dasselbe: „All das kann die KI besser als der trainierte Kardiologe, die Kardiologin oder die Rhythmologin“. Auch bei der Entscheidung, wer einen implantierbaren Defibrillator (ICD) bekommt, könne KI helfen.

Mit Blick auf Google-Entwickler Tschochohei stellte Thiele die Frage: „Wir haben ja einen Google-Software-Entwickler hier, müssen wir das alles den großen Konzernen überlassen?“ Patientinnen und Patienten gäben den großen Konzernen ohnehin schon riesige Datenmengen. Offen sei, wie Krankenhäuser und Fachgesellschaften damit umgehen. Die ESC setzt dem eigene Angebote entgegen. Dazu gehört ein Chat in ihrer App, der auf Basis der europäischen Leitlinien Vorschläge macht, wie ein einzelner Patient behandelt werden sollte. Unter ihrer neuen Präsidentin Cecilia Linde hat die ESC außerdem eine eigene Arbeitsgruppe eingerichtet, die sich um Aus- und Weiterbildung, Data Science und Leitlinien kümmert . Dort gehe es auch um die Frage, ob Leitlinien, die nur etwa alle fünf Jahre überarbeitet werden, noch zeitgemäß sind oder ob neue Modelle weiterhelfen könnten. Langfristig sehe die ESC neben Kardiologen und Rhythmologen auch Spezialisten für digitale Kardiologie und KI. So wolle die Fachgesellschaft „die Revolution der KI“ begleiten und vor allem für die Qualität sorgen.

KI beschleunigt Forschung

Clemens Scherer vom LMU Klinikum München zeigte, wie KI die Forschung beschleunigt. Beispiele waren die Vorhersage von Proteinstrukturen mit Googles AlphaFold und ein Netzwerk aus KI-Agenten, das Medikamentenkombinationen gegen akute myeloische Leukämie vorschlug. Er warnte aber vor erfundenen Quellenangaben und verwies auf Auswertungen von Nature. Große Forschungsnetzwerke wie das Deutsche Zentrum für Herz-Kreislauf-Forschung (DZHK) mit seiner Heart Bank hält er für unverzichtbar. Die Digitalisierung sei dort bisher allerdings zu kurz gekommen.

Patientensicht: „Das Monopol auf Wissen ist gefallen“

Inga Drossart ist seit fast 30 Jahren Herzpatientin und betreut als Patient Engagement Officer das Patientenforum der ESC. Sie sagte, dass allein bei ChatGPT täglich Millionen Gesundheitsfragen gestellt würden. Dass Patienten heute Zugang zu Wissen haben, hält sie für wichtig. „Die KI ersetzt den Arzt nicht und das ist auch nichts, was Patienten wollen“. Patienten suchten aber einen Berater, der sich die mitgebrachten Informationen gemeinsam mit ihnen ansieht. Digitale Gesundheitskompetenz dürfe man nicht allein den Patienten aufbürden. „So ein Patient ist keine Bedrohung“.

In der anschließenden Diskussion meldete sich der Berliner Kardiologe Benny Levenson zu Wort. Levenson führt eine Gemeinschaftspraxis in Berlin-Charlottenburg und ist Vorsitzender der Assembly of International Governors des American College of Cardiology (ACC). Er widersprach Hindricks. Dass Kliniken und Niedergelassene ihre Pfründe verteidigten, sei „ein gestriges Phänomen und ein gestriges Argument“.

Mit den Hybrid-DRGs, die der frühere Gesundheitsminister Karl Lauterbach auf den Weg gebracht hatte und bei denen ambulant und stationär gleich vergütet wird, sei man längst weiter. Das eigentliche Kernproblem sei, abgesehen davon, „dass wir digitale Analphabeten sind, insgesamt in der Versorgung“, laut Levenson, „dieses irrsinnige Problem des übersteigerten Datenschutzes“. Estland und Israel machten vor, wie es besser geht. Die Politik treibe die Entwicklung in zwei „sehr negative“ Richtungen. „Auf der einen Seite, wenn, ich komme aus einem möglicherweise demnächst linksfaschistischen Bundesland“, dort solle der Datenschutz weiter ausgebaut werden, „weil keiner irgendwas sehen darf, weil alles dem Einzelnen gehört“. Levenson erinnerte dabei an die Volkszählung in den 1980er-Jahren. Auf der anderen Seite, Richtung AfD, gebe es einen Trend, über jeden alles wissen zu wollen. Von Hindricks wollte Levenson erfahren, wie wahrscheinlich es sei, dass Deutschland bald ein so digitalisiertes Gesundheitssystem bekomme wie andere Länder.

Bezüglich der Hybrid-DRGs pflichtete Hindricks Levenson bei. Sie gingen „in die richtige Richtung und knacken die Sektoren ganz ein bisschen auf“. Dass Sektorengrenzen weiter fallen müssten, sei „unstrittig, auch unter uns“. Er sehe „viel ungerichtete Ängste auf Seiten der Politik“ und forderte mehr Mut zum Risiko. Sonst sei Deutschland international verloren. Die Fachgesellschaften müssten mehr Druck auf die Politik machen. Levenson nannte er dabei einen „der großen Protagonisten“. Themen in immer neue Kommissionen und Taskforces zu schicken, nannte er „angstbehaftetes Gehabe“. Das sei „schädlich und unerträglich und am Ende schlecht für unsere Patienten“.

Scherer sah das anders: „Meiner Meinung nach ist der Datenschutz inzwischen nicht mehr so das Problem, ehrlich gesagt, sondern einfach die technischen Möglichkeiten der Klinik“. Das LMU Klinikum ist nicht an die ePA angebunden. Die IT hat dort, wie viele weitere Kliniken ebenfalls, Sorge vor Viren, die über die ePA in die Kliniksysteme kommen. Die Sorge haben auch die Hersteller.

Auch aus anderen großen Kliniken kämen keine Einträge in der ePA an, sagte Levenson. Zudem bemängelte er den mit dem Spargesetz gefassten Beschluss der Bundesregierung, die Zusatzvergütung für die Befüllung der ePA zu streichen. „Es wird dann keiner mehr etwas in die ePA eintragen“, so Levenson. Tschochohei fragte, warum weiterhin an Arztbriefen festgehalten werde. In der Vergangenheit wurde bereits bemängelt, dass es die „Prosa“ im Brief nicht brauche, sondern die reinen Fakten ausreichten. Als Beispiel nannte er eine Patientin mit elf Arzt- und Befundbriefen, zusammen mindestens 40 Seiten Prosa. Strukturierte Daten seien hilfreicher.

Befugnisse der Krankenkassen

Eine Person aus dem Publikum warnte, der Bevölkerung sei nicht klar, dass Krankenkassen nach der neuen Gesetzgebung personenbezogen in Daten schauen dürften, etwa für Präventionsprogramme. In Zukunft sollen die Krankenkassen mit KI auch die ePA-Daten der Versicherten durchsuchen und Empfehlungen aussprechen können. Am Freitag, den 25. September, wird der Bundesrat über das Gesetz für Daten und digitale Innovation im Gesundheitswesen (GeDIG) beraten. Es soll den Kassen weitere Befugnisse geben. Geplant sind unter anderem erweiterte Möglichkeiten, Versichertendaten auszuwerten. Ärzteverbände und Patientenvertreter warnen davor, ebenso wie vor der geplanten Forschungskennziffer.

Am Rande der Veranstaltung zeigte Dr. Maximilian Priebe vom UKE, wie nah solche Technik schon beim Patienten ist. Er führte heise online die App Theodor Health vor, die er mitentwickelt hat. Man hält das Smartphone 15 Sekunden an die Brust, das Mikrofon nimmt Herz- und Lungengeräusche auf. Eine KI wertet Rhythmus, Herz- und Atemfrequenz sowie akustische Auffälligkeiten aus. Sie weist auf Unregelmäßigkeiten wie Vorhofflimmern hin und auf Herzgeräusche, die ärztlich abgeklärt werden sollten. Zusätzliche Hardware braucht es nicht. Als Medizinprodukt ist die App des Hamburger Anbieters Acus Health noch nicht zertifiziert. Das Verfahren laufe gerade, sagte Priebe.

Er forderte ein „digitales Betriebssystem für den Versorgungspfad“, dazu gehören für ihn eine eindeutige Patientenidentität und Interoperabilität, ein strukturierter Mindestdatensatz, der sich jedoch in der Entwicklung befindet, Register und Feedbackschleifen sowie Regeln für Governance und Kompetenz. Das größte Problem sei bei all den Plänen die Finanzierung. Mit der aktuellen Gesetzgebung „laufen wir eher wieder rückgängig“.

Die Vision der Charité: das Krankenhaus ohne Tastatur

Prof. Gerhard Hindricks vom Deutschen Herzzentrum der Charité (DHZC) trat deutlich offensiver auf. „Die Zukunft der Medizin wird auf digitalen Plattformen entschieden“. Für die nächsten zwei bis drei Jahre erwartet er eine deutliche Beschleunigung. Als Gründe nannte er weniger Regulierung, eine „risikoaffinere Haltung“ und Geld, denn digital aufgestellte Häuser arbeiteten wirtschaftlicher und besser. Die Technik sei nicht das Problem: „Wir haben ein Implementierungsproblem“, so Hindricks.

Künftig soll die Charité zum kontaktlosen und keyboardlosen Krankenhaus werden. Zwanzig Jahre lang habe man Ärzte vor Computer gesetzt, jetzt müsse man sie dort wieder wegholen. Im Neubau des DHZC sollen Patienten, Pflegekräfte und Ärzte freihändig sprechen und dokumentieren. Eine sprachgesteuerte „Ambient AI“ überträgt die Inhalte automatisch in die Systeme. Radarsensoren sollen Biosignale ohne Berührung erfassen. Vernetzt wird über 5G und später 6G, Hindricks verwies dazu auf die Hightech-Agenda der Bundesregierung. KI-Agenten sollen die Abläufe steuern.

Hindricks selbst arbeite schon so: „Ich erstelle keinen Arztbrief mehr, der nicht KI unterstützt ist“. Patientengespräche würden nach ausdrücklicher Zustimmung aufgezeichnet. Auf Knopfdruck gebe es zusätzlich eine Fassung in einfacher Sprache, die der Patient auch versteht. Hindricks sagte außerdem einen Durchbruch der Robotik voraus. Elon Musk möge er nicht, aber was Tesla mit autonomen, adaptiven Robotern mache, „das ist einfach unfassbar“.

„Kritik an Epic von Menschen, die nichts davon verstehen“

Zum Stand der Charité zeigte Hindricks, dass sie auf der HIMSS-Skala für den Digitalisierungsgrad (0 bis 7, hoch ist besser) derzeit auf allen Ebenen bei 0 bis 1 liege. Mit dem Krankenhausinformationssystem (KIS) Epic wolle man auf 5 bis 6 kommen und in fünf Jahren überall 6 bis 7 erreichen. Epic koste zunächst 250 Millionen Euro, „und da sind die Sekundärkosten noch nicht“ eingepreist. Im zweiten Quartal 2029 sollen rund 24.000 Beschäftigte und 3600 Betten auf einen Schlag umgestellt werden. Das sei ein „riesiges Investment“. Wenn es irgendwo ein sinnvolles Invest geben müsse, dann in der Digitalisierung des Gesundheitswesens. Für die Entscheidung sei die Charité kritisiert worden, „von Menschen, die nichts davon verstehen“. Dabei habe ein zuvor defizitäres Haus mit Epic innerhalb von zwei Jahren einen zweistelligen Millionengewinn erreicht, das Klinikum Luzern habe Ähnliches geschafft.

Das Gesundheitswesen braucht laut Hindricks selbstlernende Systeme, die mit jedem Datensatz besser werden. Die Menschen müssten verstehen, „dass da auch der individuelle Datenschutz, wo er depersonalisiert ist, komplett enden muss“. Auch die Grenzen zwischen ambulantem und stationärem Sektor müssten fallen. Krankenhäuser und Niedergelassene hielten sie teils aufrecht, um „Claims abzustecken und Kohle abzusichern, da müssen wir uns ehrlich machen“.

„KI ist besser als die kardiologische Zunft“

Laut Prof. Holger Thiele vom Herzzentrum Leipzig spricht man nicht über die Zukunft, wenn es um KI in der Rhythmusdiagnostik geht. Die KI sei besser als die kardiologische Zunft und werde das Langzeit-EKG für die Suche nach Vorhofflimmern überflüssig machen. Als Belege nannte er Studien, unter anderem aus Nature Medicine. Bei AV-Blöcken, einer gestörten Erregungsleitung zwischen Vorhof und Kammer, und anderen Befunden, gelte dasselbe: „All das kann die KI besser als der trainierte Kardiologe, die Kardiologin oder die Rhythmologin“. Auch bei der Entscheidung, wer einen implantierbaren Defibrillator (ICD) bekommt, könne KI helfen.

Mit Blick auf Google-Entwickler Tschochohei stellte Thiele die Frage: „Wir haben ja einen Google-Software-Entwickler hier, müssen wir das alles den großen Konzernen überlassen?“ Patientinnen und Patienten gäben den großen Konzernen ohnehin schon riesige Datenmengen. Offen sei, wie Krankenhäuser und Fachgesellschaften damit umgehen. Die ESC setzt dem eigene Angebote entgegen. Dazu gehört ein Chat in ihrer App, der auf Basis der europäischen Leitlinien Vorschläge macht, wie ein einzelner Patient behandelt werden sollte. Unter ihrer neuen Präsidentin Cecilia Linde hat die ESC außerdem eine eigene Arbeitsgruppe eingerichtet, die sich um Aus- und Weiterbildung, Data Science und Leitlinien kümmert . Dort gehe es auch um die Frage, ob Leitlinien, die nur etwa alle fünf Jahre überarbeitet werden, noch zeitgemäß sind oder ob neue Modelle weiterhelfen könnten. Langfristig sehe die ESC neben Kardiologen und Rhythmologen auch Spezialisten für digitale Kardiologie und KI. So wolle die Fachgesellschaft „die Revolution der KI“ begleiten und vor allem für die Qualität sorgen.

KI beschleunigt Forschung

Clemens Scherer vom LMU Klinikum München zeigte, wie KI die Forschung beschleunigt. Beispiele waren die Vorhersage von Proteinstrukturen mit Googles AlphaFold und ein Netzwerk aus KI-Agenten, das Medikamentenkombinationen gegen akute myeloische Leukämie vorschlug. Er warnte aber vor erfundenen Quellenangaben und verwies auf Auswertungen von Nature. Große Forschungsnetzwerke wie das Deutsche Zentrum für Herz-Kreislauf-Forschung (DZHK) mit seiner Heart Bank hält er für unverzichtbar. Die Digitalisierung sei dort bisher allerdings zu kurz gekommen.

Patientensicht: „Das Monopol auf Wissen ist gefallen“

Inga Drossart ist seit fast 30 Jahren Herzpatientin und betreut als Patient Engagement Officer das Patientenforum der ESC. Sie sagte, dass allein bei ChatGPT täglich Millionen Gesundheitsfragen gestellt würden. Dass Patienten heute Zugang zu Wissen haben, hält sie für wichtig. „Die KI ersetzt den Arzt nicht und das ist auch nichts, was Patienten wollen“. Patienten suchten aber einen Berater, der sich die mitgebrachten Informationen gemeinsam mit ihnen ansieht. Digitale Gesundheitskompetenz dürfe man nicht allein den Patienten aufbürden. „So ein Patient ist keine Bedrohung“.

In der anschließenden Diskussion meldete sich der Berliner Kardiologe Benny Levenson zu Wort. Levenson führt eine Gemeinschaftspraxis in Berlin-Charlottenburg und ist Vorsitzender der Assembly of International Governors des American College of Cardiology (ACC). Er widersprach Hindricks. Dass Kliniken und Niedergelassene ihre Pfründe verteidigten, sei „ein gestriges Phänomen und ein gestriges Argument“.

Mit den Hybrid-DRGs, die der frühere Gesundheitsminister Karl Lauterbach auf den Weg gebracht hatte und bei denen ambulant und stationär gleich vergütet wird, sei man längst weiter. Das eigentliche Kernproblem sei, abgesehen davon, „dass wir digitale Analphabeten sind, insgesamt in der Versorgung“, laut Levenson, „dieses irrsinnige Problem des übersteigerten Datenschutzes“. Estland und Israel machten vor, wie es besser geht. Die Politik treibe die Entwicklung in zwei „sehr negative“ Richtungen. „Auf der einen Seite, wenn, ich komme aus einem möglicherweise demnächst linksfaschistischen Bundesland“, dort solle der Datenschutz weiter ausgebaut werden, „weil keiner irgendwas sehen darf, weil alles dem Einzelnen gehört“. Levenson erinnerte dabei an die Volkszählung in den 1980er-Jahren. Auf der anderen Seite, Richtung AfD, gebe es einen Trend, über jeden alles wissen zu wollen. Von Hindricks wollte Levenson erfahren, wie wahrscheinlich es sei, dass Deutschland bald ein so digitalisiertes Gesundheitssystem bekomme wie andere Länder.

Bezüglich der Hybrid-DRGs pflichtete Hindricks Levenson bei. Sie gingen „in die richtige Richtung und knacken die Sektoren ganz ein bisschen auf“. Dass Sektorengrenzen weiter fallen müssten, sei „unstrittig, auch unter uns“. Er sehe „viel ungerichtete Ängste auf Seiten der Politik“ und forderte mehr Mut zum Risiko. Sonst sei Deutschland international verloren. Die Fachgesellschaften müssten mehr Druck auf die Politik machen. Levenson nannte er dabei einen „der großen Protagonisten“. Themen in immer neue Kommissionen und Taskforces zu schicken, nannte er „angstbehaftetes Gehabe“. Das sei „schädlich und unerträglich und am Ende schlecht für unsere Patienten“.

Scherer sah das anders: „Meiner Meinung nach ist der Datenschutz inzwischen nicht mehr so das Problem, ehrlich gesagt, sondern einfach die technischen Möglichkeiten der Klinik“. Das LMU Klinikum ist nicht an die ePA angebunden. Die IT hat dort, wie viele weitere Kliniken ebenfalls, Sorge vor Viren, die über die ePA in die Kliniksysteme kommen. Die Sorge haben auch die Hersteller.

Auch aus anderen großen Kliniken kämen keine Einträge in der ePA an, sagte Levenson. Zudem bemängelte er den mit dem Spargesetz gefassten Beschluss der Bundesregierung, die Zusatzvergütung für die Befüllung der ePA zu streichen. „Es wird dann keiner mehr etwas in die ePA eintragen“, so Levenson. Tschochohei fragte, warum weiterhin an Arztbriefen festgehalten werde. In der Vergangenheit wurde bereits bemängelt, dass es die „Prosa“ im Brief nicht brauche, sondern die reinen Fakten ausreichten. Als Beispiel nannte er eine Patientin mit elf Arzt- und Befundbriefen, zusammen mindestens 40 Seiten Prosa. Strukturierte Daten seien hilfreicher.

Befugnisse der Krankenkassen

Eine Person aus dem Publikum warnte, der Bevölkerung sei nicht klar, dass Krankenkassen nach der neuen Gesetzgebung personenbezogen in Daten schauen dürften, etwa für Präventionsprogramme. In Zukunft sollen die Krankenkassen mit KI auch die ePA-Daten der Versicherten durchsuchen und Empfehlungen aussprechen können. Am Freitag, den 25. September, wird der Bundesrat über das Gesetz für Daten und digitale Innovation im Gesundheitswesen (GeDIG) beraten. Es soll den Kassen weitere Befugnisse geben. Geplant sind unter anderem erweiterte Möglichkeiten, Versichertendaten auszuwerten. Ärzteverbände und Patientenvertreter warnen davor, ebenso wie vor der geplanten Forschungskennziffer.

Am Rande der Veranstaltung zeigte Dr. Maximilian Priebe vom UKE, wie nah solche Technik schon beim Patienten ist. Er führte heise online die App Theodor Health vor, die er mitentwickelt hat. Man hält das Smartphone 15 Sekunden an die Brust, das Mikrofon nimmt Herz- und Lungengeräusche auf. Eine KI wertet Rhythmus, Herz- und Atemfrequenz sowie akustische Auffälligkeiten aus. Sie weist auf Unregelmäßigkeiten wie Vorhofflimmern hin und auf Herzgeräusche, die ärztlich abgeklärt werden sollten. Zusätzliche Hardware braucht es nicht. Als Medizinprodukt ist die App des Hamburger Anbieters Acus Health noch nicht zertifiziert. Das Verfahren laufe gerade, sagte Priebe.

La entrada Curso online de Formación Política «Tejiendo Pedagogías Insurgentes» se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
Desde la Asamblea Internacional de los Pueblos, el Instituto Tricontinental de Investigación Social, el Instituto Transnacional (TNI) y CLACSO, les invitamos a participar del curso Tejiendo pedagogías insurgentes: geopolítica, lucha de clases y estrategias de emancipación en el Sur Global, que se realizará entre el 19 de septiembre y el 5 de diciembre de 2026.

Nuestra propuesta parte de una constatación que ya señalaba en 1990 el informe de la Comisión Sur: a pesar de los desafíos compartidos, “el Sur no conoce al Sur”. Tres décadas después, esa fragmentación persiste, mientras el capitalismo se reorganiza, el imperialismo se reconfigura y las derechas avanzan sobre nuestras conquistas.

A partir de las experiencias concretas de las luchas populares en Asia, África y América Latina y el Caribe, este curso busca contribuir a cerrar esa brecha que la distancia geográfica, la diversidad lingüística y el imperialismo interponen a la unidad del Sur Global. El proceso se concibe como un espacio de formación política orientado a fortalecer los esfuerzos organizativos de movimientos y organizaciones progresistas, poniendo en diálogo teorías, experiencias, estrategias y aprendizajes de los tres continentes.

Las y los participantes profundizarán sus conocimientos sobre cuestiones centrales del Sur Global, identificarán recursos, actores, desafíos y oportunidades, e intercambiarán a partir de las realidades concretas de sus luchas. Al ofrecer un espacio de diálogo franco y respetuoso entre la pluralidad de perspectivas de las izquierdas del Sur, el curso busca contribuir al desarrollo de una visión estratégica compartida y de una voz común, construida desde los marcos y realidades del Sur Global.

¿Cómo se organiza el curso?

El curso articulará análisis y praxis en cada sesión, integrando intervenciones teóricas con la presentación de experiencias político-organizativas concretas de los tres continentes.

Para impulsar el diálogo entre las distintas regiones, considerando nuestra diversidad lingüística y de husos horarios, cada clase contará con un/a ponente de cada región. Sus exposiciones partirán de la sistematización de las respuestas a algunas preguntas disparadoras que cada organización participante será invitada a compartir previamente.

Las respuestas podrán enviarse en árabe, francés, español, inglés o portugués. Las sistematizaciones serán compartidas en estas mismas lenguas con las organizaciones participantes y las y los ponentes.

La participación en el curso implica el compromiso de conectarse al menos al 80 % de las clases, requisito para obtener el certificado de participación emitido por CLACSO. Al mismo tiempo, invitamos a cada organización a contribuir a la construcción de una perspectiva regional desde su propio contexto y experiencia de lucha, a través de las respuestas a las preguntas disparadoras que servirán como punto de partida para las exposiciones.

La sistematización de las respuestas será compartida con las y los ponentes y con las demás organizaciones participantes, sin atribución de autoría a ninguna organización en particular. Esto permitirá que cada perspectiva pueda ser expresada con libertad y sin preocuparse por la forma: puede tratarse de una respuesta breve y objetiva o de una elaboración más extensa, por escrito o incluso mediante un mensaje de voz. Lo más importante es contar con ustedes para construir esta voz regional en toda su complejidad y diversidad.

Las clases serán cerradas y se realizarán por Zoom, siempre los sábados, de 14 a 16 h CAT. Las exposiciones de las y los ponentes, sin incluir los debates, serán grabadas y estarán disponibles en el sitio web de CLACSO. Las grabaciones completas, incluidos los debates, estarán disponibles exclusivamente para las organizaciones participantes que no hayan podido sumarse en vivo.

El curso está dirigido exclusivamente a organizaciones del Sur Global o a organizaciones internacionalistas con un trabajo relevante en el Sur Global: movimientos sociales, partidos políticos, sindicatos, colectivas, organizaciones de la sociedad civil, redes de intelectuales y activistas de África, Asia y América Latina.

Programa

Este curso es una apuesta por la unidad del Sur en un momento de profunda reorganización sistémica. Creemos que el intercambio de experiencias, teorías y estrategias entre luchas hermanas, en un espacio de confianza, constituye una oportunidad para comprender nuestra unidad en la diversidad y pensar colectivamente alternativas al desorden mundial, poniendo en el centro la vida y la solidaridad.

Por la trayectoria y relevancia de vuestra organización, nos gustaría invitarles a participar de este proceso. Sugerimos la participación de al menos dos personas por organización, para favorecer el arraigo y la continuidad de los aprendizajes. Asimismo, les pedimos contemplar la diversidad de género y, cuando sea posible, también la diversidad generacional.

In particolare, sono utili per analizzare statisticamente gli accessi o le visite al sito stesso e per consentire al titolare di migliorarne la struttura, le logiche di navigazione e i contenuti.

COOKIE DI PROFILAZIONE E SOCIAL PLUGIN

I cookie di profilazione e i social plugin, che possono essere di prima o di terza parte, servono a tracciare la navigazione dell’utente, analizzare il suo comportamento ai fini marketing e creare profili in merito ai suoi gusti, abitudini, scelte, etc. In questo modo è possibile ad esempio trasmettere messaggi pubblicitari mirati in relazione agli interessi dell’utente ed in linea con le preferenze da questi manifestate nella navigazione online.
